Class enumeration for finite mixture models with the latents R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/articles/enumeration.Rmd
enumeration.Rmd

Class enumeration refers to the process of determining the number of latent classes to be retained in an analysis. In latent profile analysis (LPA), these classes are referred to as profiles. The number of profiles is not estimated directly by the model; rather, it is specified a priori by the analyst. The model is then fitted to the data under the specified number of profiles, yielding a solution containing exactly that number. Class enumeration therefore involves fitting a sequence of models with progressively increasing numbers of profiles, typically beginning with a one-profile model, and evaluating their relative adequacy to determine which solution best represents the underlying structure of the data.

The selection of the number of profiles is consequential because it determines the structure and interpretation of the entire subsequent analysis. A model with too few profiles may combine substantively distinct groups of observations into a single profile, resulting in estimated means that adequately characterize none of the underlying groups. Conversely, a model with too many profiles may divide a genuine profile into smaller, less distinct groups that reflect sampling variability rather than meaningful heterogeneity. Additional profiles may also capture features of the measurement structure, such as residual correlations among indicators, rather than substantively distinct patterns of observations. Consequently, the number of profiles affects their estimated means, relative proportions, the assignment of observations to profiles, and the conclusions of subsequent analyses based on profile membership. In the data examined in this article, the two-profile and four-profile solutions provide different representations of the same enrolments. However, only one of these solutions corresponds to the data-generating structure, illustrating that a model with more profiles does not necessarily provide a more accurate representation of the underlying population.

In a two-level latent profile analysis, class enumeration concerns three distinct specifications, each of which must be determined by the analyst:

  • The number of profiles. Profiles represent distinct patterns of observations at the lower level, in this article course enrolments, and are defined by their means on the indicators.
  • The number of group classes. Group classes represent distinct types of groups at the upper level, in this article students, and are defined by the probability with which the observations of their groups belong to each profile. Because group classes are defined in terms of the profiles, a model with a single profile cannot contain more than one group class.
  • The covariance structure. The covariance structure determines whether the indicators are allowed to be correlated within a profile and whether profiles may differ in the size, shape and orientation of their distributions (EEI, VVI, EEE and VVV; Celeux & Govaert, 1995).

Class enumeration involves fitting and comparing models across alternative specifications of the number of profiles, the number of group classes, and the model structures under consideration. The objective is to identify the model that provides the most adequate representation of the data while accounting for model complexity and the substantive characteristics of the resulting profiles and group classes.

Conventional likelihood ratio tests are generally not appropriate for comparing finite mixture models that differ in the number of profiles or group classes. In such comparisons, the model with fewer classes can be viewed as a constrained version of the more complex model in which the probability of an additional class is fixed at zero. This restriction places the parameter on the boundary of the parameter space, violating the regularity conditions required for the usual chi-squared approximation of the likelihood ratio statistic (McLachlan, 1987). Alternative procedures include the parametric bootstrap likelihood ratio test (McLachlan, 1987) and the Lo-Mendell-Rubin approximate likelihood ratio test (Lo et al., 2001), available for supported models through bootstrap_lrt() and get_results(x, "lmr"), respectively. These tests require repeated model estimation and, consequently, careful evaluation of convergence and estimation stability.

Information criteria provide a complementary approach to model comparison by balancing model fit, typically represented by the log likelihood, against a penalty for model complexity. The Akaike information criterion (AIC; Akaike, 1974), Bayesian information criterion (BIC; Schwarz, 1978), sample-size adjusted BIC (Sclove, 1987), consistent AIC (CAIC; Bozdogan, 1987), and Kullback information criterion (KIC; Cavanaugh, 1999) incorporate penalties related to the number of estimated parameters. In contrast, the integrated classification likelihood (ICL; Biernacki et al., 2000), approximate weight of evidence (AWE; Banfield & Raftery, 1993), and classification likelihood criterion (CLC; Biernacki & Govaert, 1997) additionally account for classification uncertainty. These criteria therefore tend to favour solutions in which profiles and group classes are more clearly separated and observations can be assigned with greater certainty.

The various enumeration procedures do not necessarily identify the same model, and their relative performance depends on the characteristics of the model and the data. A simulation study by Nylund, Asparouhov, and Muthén (2007) found that the BIC and the bootstrap likelihood ratio test performed particularly well among the methods examined. Subsequent simulation research indicated that the AIC and relative entropy perform poorly in identifying the number of classes and that no criterion achieves adequate power when classes are weakly separated (Tein et al., 2013). Moreover, implementation of the Lo-Mendell-Rubin test differs between Mplus and Latent GOLD (Vermunt, 2024), highlighting the importance of considering software-specific procedures when interpreting test results.

Current recommendations therefore emphasize evaluating a range of candidate models, reporting the available fit indices and statistical tests, and integrating these results with classification diagnostics and substantive interpretability (Nylund-Gibson & Choi, 2018; Spurk et al., 2020; Weller et al., 2020; Sorgente et al., 2025). Entropy should be interpreted as a measure of classification quality for a given model rather than as a standalone criterion for determining the number of classes. The final selection should reflect the collective evidence from model fit, classification uncertainty, estimation stability, and the substantive meaningfulness of the resulting profiles and group classes. Houle et al. (2026) provide corresponding guidance for class enumeration in multilevel latent profile analysis.

These three specifications are not independent of one another and should therefore be evaluated jointly rather than sequentially. A diagonal covariance structure assumes that the indicators are uncorrelated within each profile. When this assumption is violated, the model can represent the residual association among the indicators only by introducing additional profiles, and the enumeration consequently overstates the number of profiles. In a similar manner, dependence among the observations of a group that the model does not represent, such as change across a sequence of courses, may be absorbed by additional group classes. A criterion that continues to decrease throughout the candidate range may reflect such departures from the model rather than a substantively meaningful set of profiles. For the number of group classes, the sample-size convention of the BIC is also consequential: the package reports criteria based on both the number of groups and the number of observations, and Lukočienė et al. (2010) recommend basing the choice of the number of group classes on the number of groups.

This vignette uses enumerate_classes() to fit a grid of two-level latent profile models over numbers of profiles, numbers of group classes and covariance structures. It examines information criteria, changes between adjacent candidates, descriptive curve summaries, classification diagnostics, and estimation diagnostics. Selected models are compared and a fitted candidate is extracted for further analysis. No single statistic is treated as a conclusive estimate of the number of classes.

library(latents)

Data

The examples use course_engagement, a simulated data frame in long format with one row per course enrolment. It contains 1,422 enrolments of 106 students. Five measures of activity in each course serve as indicators: browsing of the course site, lecture viewing, reading of the forum, posting to the forum and attendance. Each measure is standardized within its course, so a value of zero is the course average. The column student identifies the student to whom each enrolment belongs. The simulation is calibrated to the engagement data of students followed through a full study programme (Saqr & López-Pernas, 2021; Saqr et al., 2023). It was generated from two profiles and two kinds of students, and attendance is generated from the four click measures, so the indicators are correlated within profiles (?course_engagement).

head(course_engagement)
#>   student course sequence browse lectures forum_read forum_post attendance previous_grade

#> 2       1     19        2   0.68     0.53      -0.02      -0.55       0.70          -0.71
#> 3       1      4        3  -1.51    -0.51      -0.91      -0.80      -0.97           1.98
#> 4       1     18        4   0.64    -1.02      -1.62      -1.20      -1.26          -1.42
#> 5       1     16        5  -0.94    -0.37      -0.71      -0.28      -1.52          -0.67

#>   engagement student_type
#> 1    engaged     wavering
#> 2    engaged     wavering

#> 4 disengaged     wavering
#> 5 disengaged     wavering
#> 6 disengaged     wavering

Enrolments are nested in students. The profiles therefore describe patterns of activity in a single course, and the group classes describe students by how their enrolments are distributed across those patterns.

Fitting the candidate models

The candidates are fitted with enumerate_classes() from the data, the indicators in vars and the group identifier in id. The arguments n_profiles and n_group_classes give the numbers of classes to try, and one model is fitted for every combination of them. Here the numbers of profiles and of group classes both run from one to four. The argument model sets the covariance structure of the profiles; without it, as here, the four basic structures EEI, VVI, EEE and VVV are fitted for every combination.

Mixture likelihoods can have multiple local maxima, so each candidate is estimated from several starting values. The n_starts argument controls the number of fully fitted starts and seed controls reproducibility. This example uses five starts per candidate to limit computation. An applied analysis should assess whether increasing the number of starts changes the selected likelihood or substantive conclusions.

Every estimation argument, such as n_starts, applies identically to all candidates, and a grid is re-estimated in its entirety when more starts are required, so that every candidate has the same opportunity to reach its maximum. When many starts are used, a candidate with more profiles than the data support can reach a degenerate solution in which one profile collapses on a single observation with every variance at its lower bound; its likelihood, and hence its criteria, then depend on min_variance rather than on the data. A profile can also be spurious without reaching the bound, when a few nearly coincident observations give it variances close to zero (McLachlan & Peel, 2000, section 3.10).

A Gaussian component can concentrate around very few observations and approach a variance bound. The boundary = "exclude" option excludes starts with variances at the configured bound; it does not detect every narrowly concentrated component. The latents_thin_profiles warning flags limited posterior support relative to the number of profile-specific Gaussian parameters. This is a diagnostic heuristic rather than an identification test. Inspect component sizes and covariance diagnostics before interpreting such a profile.

The default search depends on the covariance specification. EII, EEI and EEE models use emEM screening: five times n_starts starts are screened by a short EM run each, and the first start and the best of the others, n_starts in all, are continued to convergence (Biernacki et al., 2003). The other structures start from k-means, because with profile-specific variances emEM reaches spurious maxima more often. The search argument can override these defaults. The cores argument permits parallel candidate fitting.

activity <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")
models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                            n_profiles = 1:4, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                            n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
#> 7 of 52 candidates reached their best log likelihood from one start only (profiles4_groups4_EEE, profiles4_groups1_VVV, profiles3_groups2_VVV, profiles4_groups2_VVV, profiles4_groups3_VVV, profiles3_groups4_VVV, ...); refit those you consider with more starts.

The result records 64 requested candidates. Each candidate is named by its numbers of profiles and group classes and its covariance structure, so that profiles2_groups4_VVV has two profiles, four group classes and a full covariance per profile; the name identifies the candidate in every function that follows. The 12 candidates with one profile and several group classes could not be estimated. Group classes are defined by differences in the distribution of profiles, and a model with a single profile has no such differences. These candidates remain in the table with the error that stopped them.

The columns fall into groups.

Columns Content
candidate, n_profiles, n_group_classes, model Identity of the candidate
log_likelihood, n_parameters Fit and size
aic, kic, bic_*, sabic_*, caic_*, awe_*, icl_*, clc_* Information criteria
profile_entropy, group_entropy Relative entropy at each level
avepp_min, avepp_max, avepp_mean, avepp_below Average posterior probability of the profiles
group_avepp_min, group_avepp_max, group_avepp_mean, group_avepp_below Average posterior probability of the group classes
converged, boundary, n_best_replicated, warnings, error Checks of the estimation

Information criteria

Many information criteria combine deviance (minus twice the maximized log likelihood) with a penalty for the number of estimated parameters. Some criteria also penalize classification uncertainty. Lower values are preferred under the chosen criterion. In a two-level model, several parameter penalties depend on the sample-size convention. Criteria ending in _groups count the 106 students as the independent units, and criteria ending in _individual count the 1,422 enrolments. An analysis uses one of the two conventions throughout.

ICL and AWE include uncertainty about both the students’ group classes and their enrolments’ profiles under either convention. Changing the sample-size convention changes the parameter penalty, not which classification uncertainty is included.

The candidate at the minimum of each criterion:

get_results(models, "best")
#>    criterion  convention             candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model value
#> 1        aic        <NA> profiles4_groups4_VVV          4               4   VVV 16652
#> 2        kic        <NA> profiles2_groups4_VVV          2               4   VVV 16722
#> 3        bic      groups profiles2_groups4_VVV          2               4   VVV 16798
#> 4        bic individuals profiles2_groups3_EEE          2               3   EEE 16900
#> 5      sabic      groups profiles4_groups4_VVV          4               4   VVV 16604
#> 6      sabic individuals profiles2_groups4_VVV          2               4   VVV 16770
#> 7       caic      groups profiles3_groups3_EEE          3               3   EEE 16844
#> 8       caic individuals profiles2_groups3_EEE          2               3   EEE 16930
#> 9        awe      groups profiles2_groups2_EEE          2               2   EEE 17267
#> 10       awe individuals profiles2_groups2_VVI          2               2   VVI 17412
#> 11       icl      groups profiles2_groups3_VVV          2               3   VVV 17015
#> 12       icl individuals profiles2_groups3_EEE          2               3   EEE 17122
#> 13       clc      groups profiles4_groups4_VVV          4               4   VVV 16739
#> 14       clc individuals profiles4_groups4_VVV          4               4   VVV 16739

Most criteria select two profiles; the AIC, the CLC and the SABIC with students as the units, whose parameter penalties are weakest or absent, select four, and the CAIC with students as the units three. They agree that the indicators are correlated within profiles: all but one select a structure with covariances (EEE or VVV). They disagree on the number of group classes. With students as the units, the BIC is lowest for profiles2_groups4_VVV, the ICL for profiles2_groups3_VVV and the AWE for profiles2_groups2_EEE; with enrolments as the units, the BIC is lowest for profiles2_groups3_EEE. The AIC is lowest for profiles4_groups4_VVV, the largest candidate fitted.

The covariance structure matters for the number of profiles. Among the diagonal VVI candidates alone, the BIC with students as the units is lowest for profiles4_groups3_VVI (BIC 16,852): with the within-profile correlation of attendance excluded, two further profiles absorb it. Two profiles with free covariances and two group classes fit better (BIC 16,827).

The criteria are plotted against the number of profiles, one line per number of group classes, for every structure, with the lowest value of each criterion ringed.

plot_enumeration(models)

A minimum at the largest candidate leaves uncertainty about models beyond the fitted range. Consider a wider, scientifically plausible range alongside alternative measurement and covariance specifications. An interior minimum is not guaranteed. Any criterion can be plotted by name; what = "all" displays every criterion.

plot_enumeration(models, what = "bic_groups")

The tree summarizes correspondence between profiles across independently fitted models (Zappia & Oshlack, 2018). Links are weighted by shared posterior membership mass, computed from products of the models’ membership probabilities, rather than by assuming that profiles form nested partitions. Each number of group classes and structure has its own tree; n_group_classes and model select one, and plot_tree(models) returns them all, one plot each. The guide Tree plot compares solutions at one number of profiles and plots the tree of group classes.

plot_tree(models, n_group_classes = 1, model = "VVV")

Change with each added class

When a criterion decreases across the whole candidate range, successive changes help describe how much each additional class improves that criterion. For every candidate, the table reports the decrease in BIC from the candidate with one profile fewer and the same number of group classes and structure, and the decrease from the candidate with one group class fewer. A positive value means that the added class lowered the criterion. The argument using selects another criterion.

The rows of the VVV candidates:

For the VVV structure with one group class, a second profile lowers the BIC by 343 and a third raises it by 62, which appears in the table as a negative decrease. With two profiles, a second group class lowers the BIC by 344, a third by 26 and a fourth by 3. The decreases are plotted for both directions, along the number of profiles on the left and along the number of group classes on the right.

plot_selection(models, what = "deltas")

The knee summary scales both axes of a curve to the unit interval and finds the candidate with the largest perpendicular distance below the straight line from the first point to the last. This chord-distance rule is inspired by Kneedle (Satopää et al., 2011), without its smoothing or sensitivity thresholds. A nearly linear curve can have a very small maximum distance, so the reported distance describes the strength of the bend as well as its location. The knee is computed along the number of profiles for each number of group classes, along the number of group classes for each number of profiles, and across all candidates ordered by their number of parameters, separately for each structure.

The lines of the VVV candidates:

Along the number of group classes, the knee lies at two group classes for every number of profiles from two to four and every structure; with two profiles and VVV it is profiles2_groups2_VVV, and it does not move when the largest candidate is removed (stable). The heatmap displays each candidate’s criterion value relative to the minimum across the fitted grid:

plot_selection(models, what = "heatmap")

Classification quality

Every observation has a posterior probability of membership in each class. Relative entropy summarizes these probabilities over all observations, from 0 when every observation is equally likely to belong to every class, to 1 when every observation belongs to one class with certainty (Ramaswamy et al., 1993). The average posterior probability (AvePP) of a class is the mean posterior probability of that class among the observations assigned to it. Higher AvePP values indicate greater posterior certainty within the assigned class. The candidate table reports the lowest, highest and mean AvePP at each level and the number of classes below a user-selected cutoff (cutoff, default 0.8). This threshold is a descriptive screening choice, not a validated criterion for selecting the number of classes.

plot_selection(models, what = "diagnostics")

get_results(models, "classification") returns the AvePP of every class of every candidate, with its size and the relative entropy of its level; for the VVV candidates with two profiles:

Separation of the students declines as group classes are added. With two profiles and VVV, the group-level relative entropy is 0.942 with two group classes, 0.816 with three and 0.797 with four, and the lowest group-class AvePP falls from 0.971 to 0.83.

Checks of the estimation

Replication of the selected likelihood across starts provides evidence of numerical stability, but cannot establish that the global maximum has been found. Boundary estimates and small profiles warrant investigation because they can indicate a solution driven by limited support or a restrictive parameter bound. Their interpretation depends on the fitted model and data. Refitting with boundary = "exclude" selects among starts whose continuous variance parameters are above their lower bounds. This option changes start selection and does not by itself establish that the retained profiles are substantively meaningful. The following plots summarize these diagnostics.

plot_selection(models, what = "trust")

plot_selection(models, what = "smallest")

All of the plots for choosing the number of classes are produced together with plot_selection(models).

A candidate on a boundary whose smallest profile holds about one observation is a degenerate solution, not a profile: a Gaussian profile centred on one observation raises the likelihood without limit as its variances shrink, so the reported likelihood is fixed by min_variance. The default, boundary = "allow", reports it, as Mplus does, with a warning. boundary = "exclude" retains for each candidate the best start with no variance at its lower bound, and is advisable when many starts are used, since each additional start increases the chance of reaching such a solution. Categorical indicators are unaffected.

excluded <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                              n_profiles = 1:4, n_group_classes = 1:4,
                              n_starts = 200, boundary = "exclude", seed = 1)

Comparing candidates

Selected candidates are placed side by side with compare_models(). Candidates are named as in the table or selected by a number of profiles or group classes. The comparison adds the difference in BIC from the lowest of the candidates compared and the BIC weight. The weight is exp(-delta_bic / 2) normalized over the compared candidates (Wagenmakers & Farrell, 2004). It summarizes relative support under this BIC approximation and depends on the candidate set; it should not be interpreted as a calibrated probability that a model is correct.

The candidates preferred by BIC, ICL and AWE with students as the units:

compare_models(models, "profiles2_groups4_VVV", "profiles2_groups3_VVV",
               "profiles2_groups2_EEE")

Testing neighbouring candidates

The bootstrap likelihood ratio test (McLachlan, 1987) compares two candidates that differ by one class. Data sets are simulated from the smaller candidate and both candidates are re-estimated on each. Of B requested data sets, let V pass the estimation checks and b of those yield a likelihood ratio at least as large as the observed one. The p-value is (b + 1) / (V + 1) (Davison & Hinkley, 1997); the additional count includes the observed statistic and precludes a p-value of zero. Invalid replicates are reported, and the p-value is withheld when fewer than half the requested replicates are valid. The test below compares two and three group classes with two profiles and the VVV structure, the decision on which the criteria disagree. Nineteen data sets keep the example brief; if all pass, the smallest attainable p-value is 1/20 = 0.05. Applied analyses should use at least 99 and inspect the valid count.

smaller <- get_candidate(models, "profiles2_groups2_VVV")
larger <- get_candidate(models, "profiles2_groups3_VVV")
test <- bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data = course_engagement,
                      iter = 19, n_starts = 2, seed = 1)
test
#> Parametric bootstrap likelihood-ratio comparison
#> Null: 2 profiles, 2 group classes; alternative: 2 profiles, 3 group classes
#> Observed statistic: 35.457791
#> p-value: 0.05 (Monte Carlo SE 0.0487) from 19 of 19 valid replicates (0 invalid)
plot(test)

All 19 simulated data sets are valid, and none yields a likelihood ratio as large as the observed one, so the p-value is 0.05, the smallest attainable with this number of data sets. The result therefore favours three group classes over two, in agreement with the BIC, at the smallest p-value that 19 bootstrap samples can give.

The choice

The evidence points to two profiles with free within-profile covariances. For the group classes, the bootstrap test and the BIC indicate that the data contain structure beyond two group classes. The magnitude of that structure is small: the second group class accounts for almost all of the improvement in the BIC (344 against 26 and 3 for the third and fourth), the knee lies at two group classes for every structure, and further group classes separate the students less clearly. The analysis therefore continues with profiles2_groups2_VVV, whose BIC is 29 above the lowest. The small improvements from further group classes have an identifiable source: a student’s engagement changes along the course sequence, a dependence between the enrolments of a student that the multilevel model does not represent and that additional group classes partly absorb. A latent transition model represents it directly (see the latent transition analysis article).

Analysis of the chosen candidate

The candidate is taken from the fitted candidates by name with get_candidate(). The numbers of classes with the structure give the same model, as in get_candidate(models, 2, 2, model = "VVV").

The profiles can also be related to an external variable. The following analysis uses three_step() to estimate profile-specific means of previous_grade, with the BCH correction for classification error (Bolck et al., 2004; Bakk & Vermunt, 2016). The variable precedes the course enrolment, so these comparisons describe associations rather than effects of profile membership on grades.

three_step(chosen, data = course_engagement, outcome = "previous_grade")
#> Distal outcome by class (bch, 95% CI)
#> 
#> Class   Mean          95% CI     SE  Effective n
#> -----  -----  --------------  -----  -----------
#>     1   0.23  [ 0.16,  0.30]  0.035       803.34
#>     2  -0.33  [-0.40, -0.27]  0.035       548.42

The previous grade averages 0.23 standard deviations above the mean before enrolments of the first profile and 0.33 below it before enrolments of the second, with 95% intervals that do not overlap.

Other model types

Latent class models

student_esm contains 2,582 momentary reports from students, with eight activities recorded as present or absent. Declaring the indicators in categorical makes every candidate a latent class model, and the candidates are named with classes in place of profiles.

activities <- c("time_with_friends", "on_social_media", "tv_video_games",
                "listened_music", "sports", "walking", "reading",
                "part_time_job")
lca_models <- enumerate_classes(student_esm, activities, "student",
                                n_profiles = 2:4, n_group_classes = 1:2,
                                categorical = activities, n_starts = 5,
                                seed = 1)
#> 3 of 6 candidates reached their best log likelihood from one start only (classes4_groups1, classes3_groups2, classes4_groups2); refit those you consider with more starts.
lca_models

Among the three-class models, the model with two group classes has the lower BIC. Its relative entropy is 0.53, and its least distinct class has an AvePP of 0.65. This solution was reached by a single start and lies below the maximum found with more starts in the lca vignette (log likelihood -7,695.0 against -7,678.1), so its overlapping classes reflect the search rather than the model; the two-level latent class analysis vignette analyses these data with more starts.

Single-level models

Observations without a grouping structure are modelled with enumerate_lpa() for continuous indicators and enumerate_lca() for categorical indicators. The candidates are named by their numbers of profiles or classes alone. The example below enumerates the srl data under the diagonal VVI structure, which shows how an unsuitable structure leads to degenerate candidates; the latent profile analysis workflow analyses the same data with the full EEE structure.

srl_models <- enumerate_lpa(srl, c("cognitive_strategies", "intrinsic_value",
                                   "self_efficacy", "self_regulation",
                                   "test_anxiety"),
                            n_profiles = 1:8, model = "VVI", n_starts = 10,
                            seed = 1)
#> Warning: Profile 4: 9.8 Gaussian membership mass for 10 free means and variances. This is a
#> conservative diagnostic, not an identification test; inspect the Gaussian covariance diagnostics.
#> Warning: A variance reached min_variance; this is a bound-active constrained fit.
#> Warning: Profile 3: 3.0 Gaussian membership mass for 10 free means and variances. This is a
#> conservative diagnostic, not an identification test; inspect the Gaussian covariance diagnostics.
#> Warning: A variance reached min_variance; this is a bound-active constrained fit.
#> Warning: Profiles 3, 4: 1.0, 2.0 Gaussian membership mass for 10 free means and variances each.
#> This is a conservative diagnostic, not an identification test; inspect the Gaussian covariance
#> diagnostics.
#> 2 of 8 candidates reached their best log likelihood from one start only (profiles7, profiles8); refit those you consider with more starts.
srl_models

#>  candidate n_profiles model log_likelihood n_parameters  aic bic_groups icl_individual
#>  profiles1          1   VVI          -1247           10 2515       2552           2552
#>  profiles2          2   VVI           -889           21 1821       1898           1940

#>  profiles5          5   VVI           -644           54 1397       1597           1684
#>  profiles6          6   VVI           -611           65 1351       1592           1708
#>  profiles7          7   VVI           -553           76 1258       1539           1648
#>  profiles8          8   VVI           -556           87 1285       1608           1736
#>  profile_entropy avepp_min avepp_max avepp_mean avepp_below converged boundary n_best_replicated
#>               NA        NA        NA         NA          NA      TRUE    FALSE                10
#>            0.899     0.969     0.979      0.974           0      TRUE    FALSE                10
#>            0.909     0.936     0.975      0.959           0      TRUE    FALSE                10
#>            0.859     0.885     0.954      0.917           0      TRUE    FALSE                 8
#>            0.909     0.921     0.949      0.938           0      TRUE    FALSE                 7
#>            0.892     0.886     0.959      0.934           0      TRUE    FALSE                 5
#>            0.907     0.904     0.995      0.949           0      TRUE     TRUE                 1
#>            0.897     0.896     1.000      0.937           0      TRUE     TRUE                 1
#> Every column, unrounded: as.data.frame(x).
#> No candidate is selected automatically. Compare one convention consistently.
compare_models(srl_models, "profiles5", "profiles6", "profiles7")
#> Model comparison
#> 
#> Model      Profiles   k   LogLik      BIC   ΔBIC  Weight      ICL  Entropy  Min AvePP  < 0.8
#> ---------  --------  --  -------  -------  -----  ------  -------  -------  ---------  -----
#> profiles5         5  54  -644.38  1596.76  57.27   0.000  1684.32     0.91       0.92      0
#> profiles6         6  65  -610.52  1591.78  52.30   0.000  1707.76     0.89       0.89      0
#> profiles7         7  76  -553.00  1539.48   0.00   1.000  1648.49     0.91       0.90      0
plot_selection(srl_models, what = "deltas")

BIC is minimized by profiles7, but that candidate is a boundary fit: a variance reached its lower bound, and one profile holds about 3 observations. Its low BIC reflects a nearly degenerate component, not a better description of the data. The six-profile candidate is the best fit that is not on the boundary, but it too has a profile of about 10 observations, too few to determine its own ten means and variances. The enumeration reports both with a latents_thin_profiles warning; such a profile may be a spurious maximum, and the choice should be weighed against the five-profile candidate, which compare_models() shows beside them. The eight-profile candidate is also on the boundary, with two nearly empty profiles, which marks the limit of what 300 observations can support. Every warning issued during the enumeration is retained in the warnings column of the table.

Missing values and scaled indicators

Two arguments alter the data to which the candidates are fitted and, like n_starts, apply to all candidates. With missing = "fiml", rows with some indicators missing contribute through the indicators observed (full information maximum likelihood); rows with every indicator missing are excluded from the individual sample size, entropy and AvePP, since they carry no information on class membership. centering subtracts and scaling divides by a mean or standard deviation computed over the sample ("grand") or within each group ("person"); combined, they yield grand or within-person z-scores. Information criteria are comparable only among candidates fitted under the same settings. Model selection describes both with examples.

Multiple covariance structures in single-level models

Specifying several structures in model multiplies the candidates, and the structure is appended to each name. Because the numbers of classes then match several candidates, a candidate must be specified by its full name.

crossed_models <- enumerate_lpa(srl, c("cognitive_strategies",
                                       "intrinsic_value", "self_efficacy",
                                       "self_regulation", "test_anxiety"),
                                n_profiles = 2:4, model = c("VVI", "EEE"),
                                n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
#> 1 of 6 candidates reached their best log likelihood from one start only (profiles4_EEE); refit those you consider with more starts.
crossed_models
#> Class enumeration: 6 candidate models (LPA)

Latent transition models

With time, every candidate is a latent transition model over the occasions, here the order of each student’s enrolments in sequence. As in the two-level grid above, the within-profile covariances are estimated (covariance_model = "full").

transition_models <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, activity, "student",
                                       time = "sequence",
                                       covariance_model = "full",
                                       n_profiles = 2:4, n_group_classes = 1,
                                       n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
#> 2 of 3 candidates reached their best log likelihood from one start only (profiles3_groups1, profiles4_groups1); refit those you consider with more starts.
transition_models
#> Transition-model enumeration: 3 candidates (LTA)
#>          candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model log_likelihood n_parameters   bic   aic entropy
#>  profiles2_groups1          2               1  <NA>          -8206           43 16613 16499  0.9434
#>  profiles3_groups1          3               1  <NA>          -8172           68 16662 16481  0.9462
#>  profiles4_groups1          4               1  <NA>          -8143           95 16729 16476  0.9585
#>  converged boundary
#>       TRUE    FALSE
#>       TRUE     TRUE
#>       TRUE     TRUE
#> Pick one by its name: get_candidate(x, "<candidate>").
compare_models(transition_models)
#> Model comparison
#> 
#> Model              Profiles   k    LogLik       BIC    ΔBIC  Weight       ICL  Entropy  Min AvePP  < 0.8
#> -----------------  --------  --  --------  --------  ------  ------  --------  -------  ---------  -----
#> profiles2_groups1         2  43  -8206.28  16613.08    0.00   1.000  16836.37     0.94       0.98      0
#> profiles3_groups1         3  68  -8172.26  16661.64   48.56   0.000  17006.36     0.95       0.78      1
#> profiles4_groups1         4  95  -8142.89  16728.81  115.74   0.000  17139.21     0.96       0.85      0

The BIC selects two profiles, the generating number, and every candidate converges. The latent transition analysis article enumerates profiles and group classes together.

Functions

Call Result
enumerate_classes(data, vars, id, n_profiles, n_group_classes, model) The fitted candidate models
enumerate_classes(…, n_starts = , missing = “fiml”, centering = , scaling = ) The same starts, missing-data handling, centring and scaling for every candidate
enumerate_classes(…, boundary = “exclude”) Starts with a variance at its lower bound set aside for every candidate
enumerate_classes(…, time = ), enumerate_lpa(), enumerate_lca() Transition models, single-level profile and class models
bootstrap_lrt(smaller, larger, data = , iter = ) Bootstrap likelihood ratio test of two neighbouring candidates
as.data.frame(models) One row per candidate with every column
get_results(models, “best”) The candidate at the minimum of each criterion
get_results(models, “classification”) Size, AvePP and entropy of every class of every candidate
get_results(models, “candidates”, cutoff = 0.9) The table of candidates with another AvePP cutoff
get_results(models, “deltas”, using = ) Decrease in a criterion from one profile fewer and one group class fewer
get_results(models, “knees”, using = ) Maximum chord-distance knee of each line, its range and its stability
plot_enumeration(models), plot_enumeration(models, what = “bic_groups”), what = “all” Information criteria across the candidates
plot_tree(models, n_group_classes = , model = ) Division of profiles as more are added
plot_enumeration(models, what = “entropy”, “avepp” or “diagnostics”, cutoff = ) Entropy and lowest AvePP across the candidates
plot_selection(models, what = “deltas”, “heatmap”, “smallest” or “trust”, using = ) Decreases, distance from the lowest criterion, smallest class, estimation checks
plot_selection(models) All of the plots for choosing the number of classes
get_candidate(models, “profiles2_groups2_VVV”), get_candidate(models, 2, 2, model = “VVV”) One fitted candidate
compare_models(models, “name”, label = “name”, …) Named candidates side by side
compare_models(models, n_profiles = , n_group_classes = ) All candidates with the given numbers of classes
compare_models(name = fit, name = fit) Fitted models side by side, on the same data
get_candidate(comparison, “name”) The model behind a row of a comparison
get_results(comparison, “classification”) Every class of every compared model
